transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Well, I suppose what brings me in is that I can’t seem to turn off the worrying once it gets going. I’ll tell myself, “All right, I’ve made the list, I checked the dates, I did what I could,” and then somehow my mind just keeps circling back anyway.

It’s funny, I used to be very organized—color-coded calendars, little notes on the fridge, all that—and I still do those things, but lately it doesn’t seem to settle me the way it used to. I know I’ve done what’s reasonable, but I can’t quite make myself stop thinking about it.
When these thoughts keep coming back, do they feel unwanted and intrusive, like they pop into your mind against your will?

Yes, I think so—well, maybe “intrusive” is the right word, though it’s not like a flash of something bizarre. It’s more that once the worry starts, I can’t seem to shut it off. I’ll say to myself, I made the list, I checked the dates, I’ve done everything reasonable… and then there it is again, circling back.

I used to keep everything very tidy that way—my husband used to tease me about my little notes—but now the notes don’t really quiet it down. It’s unwanted, yes. I don’t feel like I’m choosing to keep thinking about it.
When the worry comes back, do you do something over and over to try to feel better, like checking, repeating, or counting?

I don’t know that I do counting or repeating exactly. I mean, I do look back at my calendar sometimes, or I’ll glance at a note again, but that’s sort of what I’ve always done to keep myself organized.

My daughter bought me this very pretty planner last Christmas—one of those with stickers in the back, which seems a little silly at my age, but I actually liked it—and I’ll check it, yes, but I’m not sure it’s “over and over” in the way you mean. It’s more like I’m trying to reassure myself I haven’t missed something.
Are you worrying about lots of different parts of your life, or mainly about one particular problem?

It’s not just one thing, no. It sort of wanders. I’ll start thinking about the exhibition schedule—there’s a little community art thing I’ve been helping keep track of—and then somehow I’m worrying about my daughter’s travel plans, whether she’ll get stuck somewhere, and then the gutters on the house because I noticed leaves up there the other day.

It’s like each thing by itself is small, but in my head it starts to feel as if it could turn into a much bigger mess if I don’t stay on top of it.
Did this worrying start after something stressful happened in your life?

Yes, I think it did. It’s been about… seven months now, give or take. It started not long after my friend died. We had been working on a few things together—little projects, nothing grand, but they mattered to us—and I sort of tried to keep them moving after she was gone.

At first I thought I was just being responsible, you know, keeping lists and not letting things drop. She was always the one who remembered who needed to be called, which folder had what in it—funny the things you miss. But after that, the worrying just seemed to settle in and not really let up.
When the worry hits, do you feel driven to check your planner or notes again even when you know you’ve already checked enough?

I’m not sure I’d say “driven,” exactly. Sometimes I do look again, but it’s hard to tell where being careful ends and… well, where it becomes too much.

I’ve always been a notes person. Even in college I had those color-coded tabs—though now I can never find the color I want, which is ridiculous because I bought a whole pack of them. But yes, I’ll sometimes look back at the planner after I’ve already looked. I don’t always feel like I know whether that’s because I need to, or because I just don’t trust my memory in the moment.
Do these worries feel mostly connected to your friend’s death, or do they now feel separate from it?

I think it started around her death, yes, but now it doesn’t always feel tied to that directly. It’s more like my mind just keeps roaming—from the exhibition schedule to my daughter’s travel plans to whether the gutters need fixing.

And then I’ll think, well, if I don’t keep an eye on this one little thing, maybe it turns into a much bigger mess. Which sounds silly when I say it, because gutters are gutters, not… I don’t know, a catastrophe. But in my head they all start to feel connected somehow, like things could unravel if I’m not careful.
For the past six months or more, have you been worrying on most days?

Yes… most days, I’d say. It’s not always the same worry, which makes it hard to pin down. My mind just sort of roams—one minute it’s the exhibition schedule, then it’s my daughter’s travel plans, then I’m thinking about whether the house gutters need fixing.

And it starts small, but then I get this feeling that if I don’t stay on top of it, it could turn into something much bigger. Like things could unravel. I know that sounds a bit dramatic when I hear myself say it.
When the worrying starts, is it hard for you to control or stop it?

Yes, that’s really the thing that made me come in. Once it starts, I have a very hard time shutting it off.

I’ll tell myself, “You’ve made the list, you checked the dates, you’ve done what you can,” and for a little while that sounds reasonable. But then my mind sort of circles back anyway. It’s like when I used to pack for trips and I’d check the stove twice—although now I’m not even traveling much, so that’s not quite the same—but it’s that same feeling of not being able to leave it alone. Even when I know, logically, there isn’t anything more to do.
Have you been feeling restless or on edge?

Yes, I think so. Not pacing the halls exactly, but I do feel… wound up, even just sitting in my own living room.

I’ll be on the phone and notice I’m tapping my fingers, or I’ll get up to straighten a stack of papers or move a cushion, not because it really needs doing. It’s more that sitting quietly makes me feel jumpy. Funny, I used to enjoy just sitting with a cup of tea and looking out at the garden, and now I’ll suddenly think the books on the side table look crooked. But yes—on edge is probably the right word.
Do you find that you get tired easily?

Yes, I do. Even if I’ve slept right through the night, I’ll wake up feeling like I’ve already done half a day’s work, which is ridiculous because I’ve only made tea and fed myself breakfast.

And then little things tire me out more than they used to. I’ll water the garden beds—nothing strenuous, just moving the hose about—or I’ll sort some papers for book club, and afterward I need to sit down and sort of… gather myself. I used to be able to do those things without even thinking about it.
Have you been having trouble concentrating?

I’m not sure, honestly. I mean, I read the newspaper most mornings, and sometimes I realize I’ve read the same paragraph twice, but then again the paper is so full of the same unpleasant stories lately that maybe I’m just avoiding it.

I haven’t noticed it as a major thing, I don’t think. If I’m doing something straightforward, like making a grocery list or checking the mail, I manage. Though I did put the stamps in the wrong drawer last week—but that’s hardly new for me. My sister used to tease me about that years ago. So… I suppose I’d say not especially, unless you mean something more specific.
Have you been having a lot of muscle tension?

Yes, especially by the end of the day. My shoulders and neck get terribly tight, like I’ve been holding myself braced without realizing it.

Sometimes I’ll be sitting there reading, or thinking through things for the garden center activities, and I catch myself clenching my jaw. Then I think, goodness, why am I doing that? I suppose it’s like when you hold a handbag too long on one shoulder and don’t notice until afterward—though I’ve always preferred a smaller bag for that reason. But yes, the tightness is mostly in my neck and shoulders.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

I’m not sure I’d say “trouble,” exactly. I do go to bed and I have my little routine — I like the lamp on the left side because the other one flickers a bit, though I keep meaning to replace the bulb — and usually I manage well enough.

Some nights are better than others, I suppose. I might lie there a bit longer than I’d like, but I haven’t really kept track of it. My neighbor used to write down her sleep in a notebook, but that always seemed like it might make you think about it more, if you see what I mean.

So… I don’t know. I wouldn’t say I’ve noticed it as a big problem.
When you check your planner or notes again, are you doing it to prevent something bad from happening?

I suppose, yes, in a way. Not that I think the house will fall down if I don’t look at my planner again, but once the worrying starts, I can’t seem to switch it off.

I’ll tell myself, “You’ve made the list, you checked the dates, there’s nothing more to do,” and then five minutes later I’m looking again anyway. It’s a bit like when you leave the iron and wonder if you unplugged it, though I don’t really iron much anymore—most things don’t need it if you hang them properly. But yes, it’s that feeling of needing to be sure, even when I know I’ve done all I reasonably can.
When you look at your planner or notes again, does it feel like something you have to do, even though part of you knows it probably isn’t necessary?

Yes… I think that’s it. Part of me knows I’ve already made the list and checked the dates, and there isn’t anything more I can sensibly do.

But once the worry starts, it’s very hard to turn it off. I’ll go back to the planner just to settle myself, I suppose, though it doesn’t always settle me for long. It reminds me of when you reread a recipe even though you’ve made it for years—my mother used to do that with sponge cake, funny enough—but yes, with me it’s more that I feel I have to check because the worrying won’t leave me alone.
About how much time in a day do you spend checking your planner or notes?

Oh, I’m not really sure. I haven’t timed it or anything like that.

It’s sort of here and there — I might look once, then get distracted making tea or noticing the mail needs sorting, and then later I’ll glance again. So I couldn’t give you a proper number of minutes. I suppose it depends on the day, really.
On a typical day, does checking your planner or notes take more than an hour altogether?

I don’t know that I could say it adds up to more than an hour. I haven’t really sat with a clock and counted it.

It feels like little bits through the day—look at the planner, then I remember I meant to water that plant in the kitchen, or I see a note about ringing someone and then I’m off thinking about whether it’s too late in the day to call. So… altogether, I’m not sure. It might feel longer than it is, if that makes sense.
Do these repeated checks of your planner or notes interfere with your day in a significant way?

Yes, I suppose it does a bit. I still keep up with things, mostly — the garden hasn’t gone completely wild, and I do still go to book club, though last time I realized I’d only half-read the chapters because I’d spent ages fussing over what I’d written down for the week.

And with the exhibition planning, I’ve started saying no to bits I probably would’ve taken on before. It just feels harder to manage than it used to, all the dates and lists and who’s doing what. I don’t want to let anyone down, so sometimes I step back instead.
If you try not to check your planner or notes, does your anxiety rise sharply until you do?

It’s not always sharp exactly, no… not like a switch flipping. It’s more that if I try not to look, my mind keeps circling back to it.

I’ll tell myself, “You’ve made the list, you’ve checked the dates, you’ve done what you can,” and then somehow I’m still worrying about it while I’m rinsing a cup or looking out at the garden. I can’t seem to turn it off once it starts, and then checking feels like the only way to settle it a bit… though it doesn’t always last.

doctor.question: When you check your planner or notes again, are you doing it to prevent something bad from happening?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I can’t seem to turn off the worrying once it starts, even when I tell myself I’ve made the list, checked the dates, and done all I reasonably can.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether repeated checking of planner or notes is driven by anxiety about preventing something bad, which most directly relates to difficulty controlling worry once it starts.

patient.answer:
I suppose, yes, in a way. Not that I think the house will fall down if I don’t look at my planner again, but once the worrying starts, I can’t seem to switch it off.

I’ll tell myself, “You’ve made the list, you checked the dates, there’s nothing more to do,” and then five minutes later I’m looking again anyway. It’s a bit like when you leave the iron and wonder if you unplugged it, though I don’t really iron much anymore—most things don’t need it if you hang them properly. But yes, it’s that feeling of needing to be sure, even when I know I’ve done all I reasonably can.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the repeated checking is a true compulsion performed in response to obsessional doubt, which would help distinguish OCD from generalized anxiety or adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: When you look at your planner or notes again, does it feel like something you have to do, even though part of you knows it probably isn’t necessary?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I can’t seem to turn off the worrying once it starts, even when I tell myself I’ve made the list, checked the dates, and done all I reasonably can.
target_item.reason: The question is about repeatedly checking planner or notes despite knowing it is probably unnecessary, which most directly reflects difficulty stopping or controlling the worry once it starts.

patient.answer:
Yes… I think that’s it. Part of me knows I’ve already made the list and checked the dates, and there isn’t anything more I can sensibly do.

But once the worry starts, it’s very hard to turn it off. I’ll go back to the planner just to settle myself, I suppose, though it doesn’t always settle me for long. It reminds me of when you reread a recipe even though you’ve made it for years—my mother used to do that with sponge cake, funny enough—but yes, with me it’s more that I feel I have to check because the worrying won’t leave me alone.

doctor.intent: Distinguish OCD from generalized or adjustment-related anxiety by determining whether the repeated checking is time-consuming enough to suggest compulsions.
doctor.question: About how much time in a day do you spend checking your planner or notes?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the amount of time spent checking planner or notes, which is a compulsive/checking behavior duration measure; the provided symptom profile covers worry and anxiety symptoms but does not include a specific item for time spent checking.

patient.answer:
Oh, I’m not really sure. I haven’t timed it or anything like that.

It’s sort of here and there — I might look once, then get distracted making tea or noticing the mail needs sorting, and then later I’ll glance again. So I couldn’t give you a proper number of minutes. I suppose it depends on the day, really.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the checking behavior is time-consuming enough to suggest OCD rather than generalized or adjustment-related anxiety.
doctor.question: On a typical day, does checking your planner or notes take more than an hour altogether?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the amount of time spent checking planner or notes, which relates to compulsive checking/time consumption rather than any listed GAD symptom profile item.

patient.answer:
I don’t know that I could say it adds up to more than an hour. I haven’t really sat with a clock and counted it.

It feels like little bits through the day—look at the planner, then I remember I meant to water that plant in the kitchen, or I see a note about ringing someone and then I’m off thinking about whether it’s too late in the day to call. So… altogether, I’m not sure. It might feel longer than it is, if that makes sense.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the checking behavior is causing marked distress or impairment, which helps distinguish OCD from generalized anxiety or adjustment-related anxiety when time spent is unclear.
doctor.question: Do these repeated checks of your planner or notes interfere with your day in a significant way?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I still keep up with the garden and book club, but I’ve started arriving less prepared and turning down parts of the exhibition planning because it feels harder to manage than it used to.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the repeated checking significantly interferes with daily functioning, which directly maps to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Yes, I suppose it does a bit. I still keep up with things, mostly — the garden hasn’t gone completely wild, and I do still go to book club, though last time I realized I’d only half-read the chapters because I’d spent ages fussing over what I’d written down for the week.

And with the exhibition planning, I’ve started saying no to bits I probably would’ve taken on before. It just feels harder to manage than it used to, all the dates and lists and who’s doing what. I don’t want to let anyone down, so sometimes I step back instead.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the repeated checking is primarily to relieve anxiety from intrusive obsession-like thoughts rather than generalized worry, helping distinguish OCD from GAD/adjustment disorder.
doctor.question: If you try not to check your planner or notes, does your anxiety rise sharply until you do?

target_item.name: Uncontrollable_Worry
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that I can’t seem to turn off the worrying once it starts, even when I tell myself I’ve made the list, checked the dates, and done all I reasonably can.
target_item.reason: The question asks whether resisting checking causes anxiety to rise until the checking is performed, which is most directly about difficulty controlling the worry and the urge to relieve it.

patient.answer:
It’s not always sharp exactly, no… not like a switch flipping. It’s more that if I try not to look, my mind keeps circling back to it.

I’ll tell myself, “You’ve made the list, you’ve checked the dates, you’ve done what you can,” and then somehow I’m still worrying about it while I’m rinsing a cup or looking out at the garden. I can’t seem to turn it off once it starts, and then checking feels like the only way to settle it a bit… though it doesn’t always last.

opening_question.intent: Identify the patient's main presenting problem in their own words
opening_question.question: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient describes excessive anxiety and worry about multiple domains on most days for about 7 months, with difficulty controlling the worry and associated symptoms of restlessness, fatigue, and muscle tension, along with functional impact. Although the symptoms began after a psychosocial stressor (friend's death) and there is some reassurance-seeking/checking behavior, the worry is now generalized across several life areas rather than primarily tied to the stressor, and the checking does not clearly meet OCD thresholds such as distinct obsessions/compulsions consuming substantial time. This most strongly supports generalized anxiety disorder.
